claim: Amygdalin is a cyanogenic glycoside found in honey bee-pollinated almond trees.
source: In this study, we show that amygdalin, a cyanogenic glycoside found in honey bee-pollinated almond trees, can be metabolized by both bees and members of the gut microbiota.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this in the abstract, and this is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: Amygdalin can be metabolized by both bees and members of the gut microbiota.
source: In this study, we show that amygdalin, a cyanogenic glycoside found in honey bee-pollinated almond trees, can be metabolized by both bees and members of the gut microbiota.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data from both in vitro and in vivo experiments.

claim: In microbiota-deprived bees, amygdalin is degraded into prunasin, leading to prunasin accumulation in the midgut and hindgut.
source: In microbiota-deprived bees, amygdalin is degraded into prunasin, leading to prunasin accumulation in the midgut and hindgut.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data from in vivo experiments showing prunasin detection in microbiota-deprived bees (Figure 8D-E).

claim: In microbiota-colonized bees, amygdalin is degraded even further, and prunasin does not accumulate in the gut.
source: In microbiota-colonized bees, on the other hand, amygdalin is degraded even further, and prunasin does not accumulate in the gut, suggesting that the microbiota contribute to the full degradation of amygdalin into hydrogen cyanide.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data from in vivo experiments showing no prunasin accumulation in microbiota-colonized bees (Figure 8D-E).

claim: The microbiota contribute to the full degradation of amygdalin into hydrogen cyanide.
source: In microbiota-colonized bees, on the other hand, amygdalin is degraded even further, and prunasin does not accumulate in the gut, suggesting that the microbiota contribute to the full degradation of amygdalin into hydrogen cyanide.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that prunasin does not accumulate in microbiota-colonized bees, suggesting further degradation.

claim: Amygdalin degradation by bee gut bacteria is strain-specific and not characteristic of a particular genus or species.
source: In vitro experiments demonstrated that amygdalin degradation by bee gut bacteria is strain-specific and not characteristic of a particular genus or species.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro experiments showing variation in amygdalin degradation among different strains within the same genus (Figure 1).

claim: Strains of Bifidobacterium, Bombilactobacillus, and Gilliamella can degrade amygdalin.
source: We found strains of Bifidobacterium, Bombilactobacillus, and Gilliamella that can degrade amygdalin.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro experiments showing amygdalin degradation by specific strains (Figure 1H-J).

claim: The degradation mechanism of amygdalin appears to vary since only some strains produce prunasin as an intermediate.
source: The degradation mechanism appears to vary since only some strains produce prunasin as an intermediate.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data showing prunasin production in some strains but not others (Figure 1L-O, Figure 2).

claim: Bifidobacterium wkB204 fully degrades amygdalin.
source: Finally, we investigated the basis of degradation in Bifidobacterium wkB204, a strain that fully degrades amygdalin.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data showing complete amygdalin degradation in wkB204 cultures (Figure 1H).

claim: Bifidobacterium wkB204 overexpresses and secretes several carbohydrate-degrading enzymes when grown with amygdalin.
source: We found overexpression and secretion of several carbohydrate-degrading enzymes, including one in glycoside hydrolase family 3 (GH3).
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data showing differential protein expression in amygdalin-grown cultures (Figure 4C).

claim: A glycoside hydrolase family 3 (GH3) enzyme from Bifidobacterium wkB204 contributes to amygdalin degradation.
source: We expressed this GH3 in Escherichia coli and detected prunasin as a byproduct when cell lysates were cultured with amygdalin, supporting its contribution to amygdalin degradation.
evidence: This is supported by heterologous expression experiments showing prunasin production when E. coli expressing the GH3 is incubated with amygdalin (Figure 7D-E).

claim: Both host and microbiota can act together to metabolize dietary plant metabolites.
source: These findings demonstrate that both host and microbiota can act together to metabolize dietary plant metabolites.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by in vivo experiments showing partial degradation by the host and complete degradation with the microbiota.

claim: The bee genome has lower detoxification gene diversity than the genomes of other insects.
source: Although the bee genome encodes enzymes that help in the metabolism of xenobiotics, it has lower detoxification gene diversity than the genomes of other insects.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous genomic studies (Berenbaum and Johnson, 2015; Sadd et al., 2015).

claim: Bees may rely on the microbiota to degrade potentially toxic molecules.
source: Therefore, bees may rely on other components that shape their physiology, such as the microbiota, to degrade potentially toxic molecules.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that bees have lower detoxification gene diversity and the experimental findings showing microbiota contribution to amygdalin degradation.

claim: Amygdalin is present in nectar and pollen of almond trees.
source: Studies on almonds show that amygdalin is present in nectar and pollen (London-Shafir et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The western honey bee, Apis mellifera, is the primary pollinator of almonds.
source: The western honey bee, Apis mellifera, is the primary pollinator of almonds and likely also encounters amygdalin in other crops.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of apiculture and agriculture.

claim: The toxicity of amygdalin derives from its degradation products.
source: The toxicity of amygdalin derives from its degradation products (Jaszczak-Wilke et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: During degradation, amygdalin is usually first broken down into prunasin and a glucose molecule.
source: During degradation, amygdalin is usually first broken down into prunasin and a glucose molecule.
evidence: This is established knowledge about amygdalin degradation pathways.

claim: Prunasin is broken down into another glucose molecule and mandelonitrile.
source: Then, prunasin is broken down into another glucose molecule and mandelonitrile, with the latter compound converted into benzaldehyde and hydrogen cyanide.
evidence: This is established knowledge about amygdalin degradation pathways.

claim: Mandelonitrile is converted into benzaldehyde and hydrogen cyanide.
source: Then, prunasin is broken down into another glucose molecule and mandelonitrile, with the latter compound converted into benzaldehyde and hydrogen cyanide.
evidence: This is established knowledge about amygdalin degradation pathways.

claim: Hydrogen cyanide is a toxic molecule that can lead to acute poisoning in animals.
source: Hydrogen cyanide is a toxic molecule that can lead to acute poisoning in animals (Khandekar and Edelman, 1979; Carter et al., 1980; Newton et al., 1981; Kolesarova et al., 2021; Kovacikova et al., 2019; Salama et al., 2019) as it interferes with the electron transport chain during oxidative phosphorylation (Cooper and Brown, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Hydrogen cyanide interferes with the electron transport chain during oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Hydrogen cyanide is a toxic molecule that can lead to acute poisoning in animals (Khandekar and Edelman, 1979; Carter et al., 1980; Newton et al., 1981; Kolesarova et al., 2021; Kovacikova et al., 2019; Salama et al., 2019) as it interferes with the electron transport chain during oxidative phosphorylation (Cooper and Brown, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Some bees are not deterred by amygdalin concentrations encountered in almond nectar (up to 15 μM).
source: Interestingly, some bees are not deterred by amygdalin concentrations encountered in almond nectar (up to 15 μM) (London-Shafir et al., 2003; Stevenson et al., 2017), and can tolerate concentrations up to 219 μM with no effects on survivorship (Irwin et al., 2014; Lecocq et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Bees can tolerate amygdalin concentrations up to 219 μM with no effects on survivorship.
source: Interestingly, some bees are not deterred by amygdalin concentrations encountered in almond nectar (up to 15 μM) (London-Shafir et al., 2003; Stevenson et al., 2017), and can tolerate concentrations up to 219 μM with no effects on survivorship (Irwin et al., 2014; Lecocq et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Concentrations of amygdalin in almond pollen can reach up to 4 mM.
source: Bees feeding on particular plants may be exposed to even higher doses of amygdalin; for example, concentrations in almond pollen can reach up to 4 mM (London-Shafir et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Exposure to high doses of amygdalin leads to acute malaise symptoms in bees, including a sharp increase in time spent upside down and abdomen dragging.
source: Exposure to these high doses of amygdalin leads to acute malaise symptoms, including a sharp increase in time spent upside down and abdomen dragging (Hurst et al., 2014), and exposure for several days lowers bee survivorship (Kevan and Ebert, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Exposure to amygdalin for several days lowers bee survivorship.
source: Exposure to these high doses of amygdalin leads to acute malaise symptoms, including a sharp increase in time spent upside down and abdomen dragging (Hurst et al., 2014), and exposure for several days lowers bee survivorship (Kevan and Ebert, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Lower doses of amygdalin can result in lower survivorship in lab trials.
source: Lower doses can also result in lower survivorship in lab trials (Ayestaran et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Colony-level exposure to amygdalin may protect bees against parasites, such as the trypanosomatid Lotmaria passim.
source: Despite the potential for toxicity to bees, colony-level exposure to amygdalin may protect bees against parasites, such as the trypanosomatid Lotmaria passim (Tauber et al., 2020), and may reduce the titer of some pathogenic viruses (Tauber et al., 2020; Palmer-Young et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Amygdalin may reduce the titer of some pathogenic viruses in bees.
source: Despite the potential for toxicity to bees, colony-level exposure to amygdalin may protect bees against parasites, such as the trypanosomatid Lotmaria passim (Tauber et al., 2020), and may reduce the titer of some pathogenic viruses (Tauber et al., 2020; Palmer-Young et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The genomes of honey bees and bumble bees have fewer detoxification genes compared to other insects.
source: The genomes of honey bees and bumble bees have fewer detoxification genes compared to other insects (Berenbaum and Johnson, 2015; Sadd et al., 2015), but they do encode some enzymes that can degrade plant metabolites, such as cytochrome P450 monooxygenases, glutathione transferases, and GHs (Berenbaum and Johnson, 2015; Pontoh and Low, 2002; Rand et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous genomic studies.

claim: Bee genomes encode enzymes that can degrade plant metabolites, such as cytochrome P450 monooxygenases, glutathione transferases, and glycoside hydrolases.
source: The genomes of honey bees and bumble bees have fewer detoxification genes compared to other insects (Berenbaum and Johnson, 2015; Sadd et al., 2015), but they do encode some enzymes that can degrade plant metabolites, such as cytochrome P450 monooxygenases, glutathione transferases, and GHs (Berenbaum and Johnson, 2015; Pontoh and Low, 2002; Rand et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Honey bees secrete a glycoside hydrolase into their mouths from their hypopharyngeal glands that is then transferred to the midgut.
source: For example, honey bees secrete a GH into their mouths from their hypopharyngeal glands that is then transferred to the midgut where it can potentially catalyze the initial breakdown of glycosides (Pontoh and Low, 2002; Ricigliano et al., 2017), such as the conversion of amygdalin into prunasin.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Amygdalin toxicity occurs after ingestion, but not after injection into the hemolymph.
source: Amygdalin toxicity occurs after ingestion, but not after injection into the hemolymph (Hurst et al., 2014), suggesting that enzymes in the gut achieve the conversion of amygdalin into hydrogen cyanide.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Enzymes in the gut achieve the conversion of amygdalin into hydrogen cyanide.
source: Amygdalin toxicity occurs after ingestion, but not after injection into the hemolymph (Hurst et al., 2014), suggesting that enzymes in the gut achieve the conversion of amygdalin into hydrogen cyanide.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that amygdalin is toxic when ingested but not when injected.

claim: The dominant bee gut bacterial species produce a vast arsenal of glycoside hydrolases.
source: The latter possibility is suggested by the vast arsenal of GHs produced by the dominant bee gut bacterial species (Zheng et al., 2019; Ellegaard et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Amygdalin itself does not show antibacterial effects in vitro.
source: Interestingly, amygdalin itself does not show antibacterial effects in vitro, and the honey bee gut microbiota appears not to be significantly affected by amygdalin exposure (Tauber et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The honey bee gut microbiota appears not to be significantly affected by amygdalin exposure.
source: Interestingly, amygdalin itself does not show antibacterial effects in vitro, and the honey bee gut microbiota appears not to be significantly affected by amygdalin exposure (Tauber et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study and confirmed by the authors' own data (Figure 9C-E).

claim: Breakdown of amygdalin to prunasin is achieved by hosts without a microbiota.
source: We found that breakdown to prunasin is achieved by hosts without a microbiota and that further degradation can be performed by specific strains of dominant microbiota species.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo experiments showing prunasin accumulation in microbiota-deprived bees (Figure 8D-E).

claim: Further degradation of prunasin can be performed by specific strains of dominant microbiota species.
source: We found that breakdown to prunasin is achieved by hosts without a microbiota and that further degradation can be performed by specific strains of dominant microbiota species.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo experiments showing no prunasin accumulation in microbiota-colonized bees (Figure 8D-E).

claim: Bifidobacterium strain wkB204 grew in the presence of amygdalin as the sole carbon source.
source: Strain wkB204 grew in the presence of amygdalin as the sole carbon source, suggesting that this strain degrades amygdalin and is not susceptible to the potential byproducts (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by growth data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Bifidobacterium strains wkB344 and wkB338 grew only when glucose was added, and their growth was hampered if amygdalin was added.
source: On the other hand, strains wkB344 and wkB338 grew only when glucose was added, and their growth was hampered if amygdalin was added, indicating a toxic effect on these strains (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by growth data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Bombilactobacillus strains BI-1.1 and BI-2.5 grew in the presence of amygdalin as the sole carbon source.
source: Strains BI-1.1 and BI-2.5 grew in the presence of amygdalin as the sole carbon source, with BI-2.5 growing better than BI-1.1.
evidence: This is supported by growth data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Growth of Bombilactobacillus strain BI-2.5 was higher with amygdalin than with glucose as the sole carbon source.
source: In fact, growth of BI-2.5 was higher with amygdalin than with glucose as the sole carbon source (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by growth data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Bombilactobacillus strains LV-8.1 and Bin4N grew only in the medium with glucose, but their growth was not affected when amygdalin was added.
source: Strains LV-8.1 and Bin4N grew only in the medium with glucose, but their growth was not affected when amygdalin was added (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by growth data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Most Gilliamella strains grew at similar rates in the presence or absence of 10 mM amygdalin, except for wkB108 and wkB1 which exhibited a delay in growth.
source: Most of the strains grew at similar rates in the presence or absence of 10 mM amygdalin, except for wkB108 and wkB1 which exhibited a delay in growth, suggesting susceptibility to amygdalin at the tested concentration (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by growth data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: All Lactobacillus nr. melliventris strains grew in the presence of amygdalin, though HB-2 growth was reduced by adding amygdalin to MRS.
source: All strains grew in the presence of amygdalin, though HB-2 growth was reduced by adding amygdalin to MRS (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by growth data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: For most bacterial strains tested, growth was hampered by increasing the concentration of amygdalin from 10 to 100 mM.
source: For most bacterial strains tested, growth was hampered by increasing the concentration of amygdalin from 10 to 100 mM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by growth data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Amygdalin degradation was confirmed for Bifidobacterium strain wkB204 and Bombilactobacillus strains BI-1.1 and BI-2.5.
source: Using LC-MS analyses, amygdalin degradation was confirmed for strains that could grow in the presence of amygdalin as the sole carbon source, such as Bifidobacterium strain wkB204 (Figure 1H) and Bombilactobacillus strains BI-1.1 and BI-2.5 (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 1H-I.

claim: Bombilactobacillus strain BI-2.5 degrades less amygdalin when glucose is also present in the medium.
source: Interestingly, Bombilactobacillus strain BI-2.5 degrades less amygdalin when glucose is also present in the medium (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: For Bifidobacterium strain wkB204 and Bombilactobacillus strain BI-1.1, similar levels of amygdalin degradation were detected in cultures with or without glucose.
source: For Bifidobacterium strain wkB204 and Bombilactobacillus strain BI-1.1, on the other hand, similar levels of amygdalin degradation were detected in cultures with or without glucose (Figure 1H–I).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 1H-I.

claim: Amygdalin degradation was observed only for Gilliamella strain wkB112.
source: We observed amygdalin degradation only for Gilliamella strain wkB112 (Figure 1J and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 1J and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Metabolism of amygdalin by Bifidobacterium strain wkB204 and Bombilactobacillus strain BI-1.1 produces prunasin as a byproduct.
source: Metabolism of amygdalin by Bifidobacterium strain wkB204 and Bombilactobacillus strain BI-1.1 produces prunasin as a byproduct (Figure 1L–M and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–H), although prunasin was only detected in wkB204 cultures after providing an excessive amount of amygdalin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 1L-M and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G-H.

claim: Prunasin was not produced by Bombilactobacillus strain BI-2.5 or Gilliamella strain wkB112.
source: On the other hand, prunasin was not produced by Bombilactobacillus strain BI-2.5 or Gilliamella strain wkB112 (Figure 1M–N) even after adding excess amygdalin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H–I).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 1M-N and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H-I.

claim: Bombilactobacillus strain BI-2.5 and Gilliamella strain wkB112 metabolize amygdalin by breaking down the glycosidic bond that links the two glucose residues to the aglycone, releasing a disaccharide and mandelonitrile into the medium.
source: Therefore, BI-2.5 and wkB112 seem to metabolize amygdalin in a different way than wkB204 and BI-1.1, probably by breaking down the glycosidic bond that links the two glucose residues to the aglycone, releasing a disaccharide and mandelonitrile into the medium.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that these strains do not produce prunasin as an intermediate.

claim: Amygdalin breakdown via a prunasin intermediate is limited to Bifidobacterium strain wkB204 and Bombilactobacillus strain BI-1.1.
source: These results suggest that amygdalin breakdown via a prunasin intermediate is limited to wkB204 and BI-1.1.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data showing prunasin production only in these strains (Figure 2).

claim: The enzyme involved in amygdalin degradation by Bifidobacterium strain wkB204 is secreted.
source: After finding that specific strains from different bee gut bacterial species can degrade amygdalin, we focused on honey bee-associated Bifidobacterium strains to investigate the enzyme involved in this metabolism. First, we checked whether the enzyme is secreted or not.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assays showing amygdalin degradation in spent medium (Figure 3B).

claim: Spent medium of wkB204 amygdalin-grown cultures achieved full degradation of amygdalin.
source: Since spent medium of wkB204 amygdalin-grown cultures achieved full degradation of amygdalin, we decided to characterize the secreted enzyme involved in the degradation.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assays shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Amygdalin-grown cultures of Bifidobacterium strain wkB204 had a distinct secretome when compared to glucose-grown cultures.
source: Protein profiles were first obtained by SDS-PAGE gel and showed that amygdalin-grown cultures had a distinct secretome when compared to glucose-grown cultures (Figure 4B, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by SDS-PAGE gel data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 107 proteins were secreted in higher abundance in amygdalin-grown cultures of Bifidobacterium strain wkB204 compared to glucose-grown cultures.
source: Then, samples were submitted to proteomics analysis, which confirmed the expression differences, as we found 107 proteins secreted in higher abundance in amygdalin-grown cultures and 131 proteins secreted in higher abundance in glucose-grown cultures (p<0.05, t-test followed by Benjamini-Hochberg procedure to control for false discovery, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 131 proteins were secreted in higher abundance in glucose-grown cultures of Bifidobacterium strain wkB204 compared to amygdalin-grown cultures.
source: Then, samples were submitted to proteomics analysis, which confirmed the expression differences, as we found 107 proteins secreted in higher abundance in amygdalin-grown cultures and 131 proteins secreted in higher abundance in glucose-grown cultures (p<0.05, t-test followed by Benjamini-Hochberg procedure to control for false discovery, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Several significantly upregulated proteins in amygdalin-grown cultures of Bifidobacterium strain wkB204 are associated with carbohydrate metabolism.
source: Several significantly upregulated proteins in amygdalin-grown cultures are associated with carbohydrate metabolism (Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4—source data 2.

claim: A highly expressed enzyme belonging to the glycoside hydrolase family 3 (GH3) (WP_254476944) was detected only in amygdalin-grown cultures of Bifidobacterium strain wkB204.
source: Interestingly, we detected a highly expressed enzyme belonging to the glycoside hydrolase family 3 (GH3) (WP_254476944) only in amygdalin-grown cultures (Figure 4C), suggesting its involvement in the observed degradation.
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Specific bacterial or fungal GH3 enzymes can degrade amygdalin.
source: Other studies have demonstrated that specific bacterial or fungal GH3 enzymes can degrade amygdalin (Gao and Wakarchuk, 2014; Guo et al., 2015; Chang and Zhang, 2012; Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ten other Bifidobacterium strains encode a GH3 in their genomes with a high sequence similarity to the wkB204 GH3.
source: Ten other Bifidobacterium strains encode a GH3 in their genomes with a high sequence similarity to the wkB204 GH3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by BLAST search results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bifidobacterium strain wkB344 encodes a GH3 (WP_121913979) with high sequence similarity to the wkB204 GH3.
source: Intriguingly, these included a GH3 from wkB344 (WP_121913979), which did not grow in the presence of amygdalin in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis and phylogenetic data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In the presence of glucose as the sole carbon source, Bifidobacterium strains wkB204 and wkB344, but not wkB338, express the GH3 gene.
source: In the presence of glucose as the sole carbon source, strains wkB204 and wkB344, but not wkB338, express the GH3 gene (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: When cultivated in the presence of amygdalin as the sole carbon source, only Bifidobacterium strain wkB204 shows elevated expression of GH3 transcripts.
source: When cultivated in the presence of amygdalin as the sole carbon source, only wkB204 shows elevated expression of GH3 transcripts (Figure 5B), which correlates with the ability of this strain to degrade amygdalin in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The wkB204 GH3 (WP_254476944) is encoded in an operon containing four other genes: a major facilitator superfamily transporter (WP_254476943), a glycoside hydrolase family 30 (WP_254477160), and a beta-galactosidase (WP_254477161).
source: The wkB204 GH3 (WP_254476944), which is overexpressed in amygdalin-grown cultures, is encoded in an operon containing four other genes: a major facilitator superfamily transporter (WP_254476943), a glycoside hydrolase family 30 (WP_254477160), and a beta-galactosidase (WP_254477161) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The genes in the wkB204 GH3 operon were also overexpressed in the presence of amygdalin, based on proteomics data.
source: These were also overexpressed in the presence of amygdalin, based on proteomics data (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The wkB344 GH3 (WP_121913979) is encoded in an operon with a beta-galactosidase (WP_121914045) as the only other gene in the operon.
source: The wkB344 GH3 (WP_121913979) is also encoded in an operon, but a beta-galactosidase (WP_121914045) is the only other gene in the operon (Figure 5C), as predicted by the operon-mapper webserver (Taboada et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The genome of Bifidobacterium strain wkB204 encodes 10 distinct GH3s.
source: According to the dbCAN meta server for automated CAZyme annotation, the genomes of these three Bifidobacterium strains encode multiple GH3s: wkB204 encodes 10 distinct GH3s, while wkB344 and wkB338 encode 5 distinct GH3s each (Figure 5—source data 1; Yin et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis using the dbCAN meta server.

claim: The genomes of Bifidobacterium strains wkB344 and wkB338 encode 5 distinct GH3s each.
source: According to the dbCAN meta server for automated CAZyme annotation, the genomes of these three Bifidobacterium strains encode multiple GH3s: wkB204 encodes 10 distinct GH3s, while wkB344 and wkB338 encode 5 distinct GH3s each (Figure 5—source data 1; Yin et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis using the dbCAN meta server.

claim: All Bifidobacterium strains wkB204, wkB344, and wkB338 can degrade prunasin.
source: To investigate whether Bifidobacterium strains can also degrade prunasin, we performed an additional in vitro experiment in which Bifidobacterium strains wkB204, wkB344, and wkB338 were grown in 10 mM glucose in SDM in the presence of 0.1 mM prunasin (Figure 6A). Under these conditions, all strains grew in the presence of prunasin (Figure 6B) and degraded it (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by growth and LC-MS data shown in Figure 6B-C.

claim: Bifidobacterium strain wkB344 can degrade 0.1 mM amygdalin.
source: For comparison, we also checked growth in the presence of 0.1 mM amygdalin (Figure 6D) and found that not only wkB204, but also wkB344 degraded amygdalin (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The lack of growth and degradation observed for Bifidobacterium strain wkB344 at higher amygdalin concentrations is probably due to the much higher concentration of amygdalin provided in previous cultures (10 or 100 mM).
source: The lack of growth and, consequently, of degradation observed before for this strain is probably due to the much higher concentration of amygdalin provided in previous cultures (10 or 100 mM).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that wkB344 can degrade amygdalin at lower concentrations but not at higher concentrations.

claim: Cell lysates of transformed E. coli expressing wkB204-GH3 or wkB344-GH3 degraded amygdalin and produced prunasin.
source: After 5 days of incubation, we observed amygdalin degradation (Figure 7D) followed by prunasin production (Figure 7E) for E. coli cell lysates expressing either wkB204-GH3 or wkB344-GH3, but not for E. coli transformed with an empty plasmid, indicating that both enzymes can degrade amygdalin into prunasin.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 7D-E.

claim: The Bifidobacterium-related GH3 enzyme can degrade prunasin, but to a lesser extent than amygdalin under the tested conditions.
source: When the cell lysates were incubated in the presence of prunasin, only a small amount of prunasin was degraded (Figure 7F), suggesting that this enzyme, under the tested conditions, still can degrade prunasin, but to a lesser extent.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Amygdalin was detected in different compartments of the bee body, including the midgut, the hindgut and the body carcass without the gut of microbiota-deprived, conventionalized, and monocolonized bees.
source: Amygdalin was detected in different compartments of the bee body, including the midgut, the hindgut and the body carcass without the gut of MD, CV, and monocolonized bees (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: In the hindgut samples, amygdalin was detected for microbiota-deprived and wkB344-monocolonized bees but not for conventionalized and wkB204-monocolonized bees.
source: In the hindgut samples, amygdalin was detected for MD and wkB344-monocolonized bees but not for CV and wkB204-monocolonized bees (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Total amygdalin concentration was significantly lower in conventionalized bees and wkB204-monocolonized bees when compared to control bees not treated with amygdalin but spiked with 5 μL of 1 mM amygdalin during the extraction protocol.
source: Total amygdalin concentration was significantly lower in CV bees and wkB204-monocolonized bees when compared to control bees not treated with amygdalin but spiked with 5 μL of 1 mM amygdalin during the extraction protocol (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Prunasin was only detected in the midgut and hindgut of microbiota-deprived bees.
source: Interestingly, prunasin was only detected in the midgut and hindgut of MD bees (Figure 8D–E).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 8D-E.

claim: The presence of the microbiota contributes to continued amygdalin and prunasin degradation in the bee gut.
source: Therefore, the presence of the microbiota contributes to continued amygdalin and prunasin degradation in the bee gut.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that amygdalin concentration is reduced and prunasin does not accumulate in microbiota-colonized bees.

claim: Honey bees exposed to concentrations of amygdalin, ranging from 0.01 to 1 mM, did not exhibit increased mortality rates or dysbiosis.
source: Honey bees exposed to concentrations of amygdalin, ranging from 0.01 to 1 mM, did not exhibit increased mortality rates or dysbiosis (Figure 9A–B).
evidence: This is supported by survival data and microbiome analysis shown in Figure 9A-B.

claim: No significant changes were found in gut microbial composition of amygdalin-treated bees when compared to untreated bees.
source: We did not find any significant changes in gut microbial composition (Figure 9C–D) or abundance (Figure 9E) of amygdalin-treated bees when compared to untreated bees, which is consistent with other studies (Tauber et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing data shown in Figure 9C-D.

claim: No significant changes were found in gut microbial abundance of amygdalin-treated bees when compared to untreated bees.
source: We did not find any significant changes in gut microbial composition (Figure 9C–D) or abundance (Figure 9E) of amygdalin-treated bees when compared to untreated bees, which is consistent with other studies (Tauber et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 9E.

claim: Amygdalin did not affect mortality rates of microbiota-deprived bees.
source: Moreover, amygdalin did not affect mortality rates of MD bees (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: The concentrations used in the in vivo experiments are below the concentrations detected in almond pollen (~4 mM).
source: The concentrations used in the in vivo experiments are below the concentrations detected in almond pollen (~4 mM), and the lower concentration resembles what has been detected in almond nectar (~0.01 mM) (London-Shafir et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental concentrations to field-relevant concentrations from the literature.

claim: Dietary compounds can be metabolized not only by host enzymes but also by the gut microbiota, potentially resulting in increased or decreased toxicity.
source: Dietary compounds can be metabolized not only by host enzymes but also by the gut microbiota, potentially resulting in increased or decreased toxicity (Koppel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous review.

claim: The findings for honey bees parallel those for the metabolism of amygdalin in rats, in which the molecule is degraded to produce toxic hydrogen cyanide only in the presence of the gut microbiota.
source: Our findings for honey bees parallel those for the metabolism of amygdalin in rats, in which the molecule is degraded to produce toxic hydrogen cyanide only in the presence of the gut microbiota, but not when microbiota is absent or when injected (Carter et al., 1980).
evidence: This is a comparison to findings from a previous study in rats.

claim: Specific members of the bee gut microbiota produce a diverse set of carbohydrate digestive enzymes, including pectin lyases and glycoside hydrolases, that help in food processing.
source: Specific members of the bee gut microbiota produce a diverse set of carbohydrate digestive enzymes, including pectin lyases (PLs) and GHs, that help in food processing (Zheng et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2016; Engel et al., 2012) and detoxification (Berenbaum and Johnson, 2015; Koch et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Gilliamella strains produce pectin lyases and glycoside hydrolases that are involved in the metabolism of pectin and hemicellulose from the pollen cell wall and toxic sugars from nectar or produced during digestion of pectin.
source: For instance, Gilliamella strains produce PLs and GHs that are involved in the metabolism of pectin and hemicellulose from the pollen cell wall and toxic sugars from nectar or produced during digestion of pectin (Zheng et al., 2016; Engel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Some sugars, such as mannose, arabinose, xylose, and galactose, are indigestible for bees and can cause toxicity if accumulated in the gut.
source: Some of these sugars, such as mannose, arabinose, xylose, and galactose, are indigestible for bees and can cause toxicity if accumulated in the gut (Barker, 1977).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Bombilactobacillus and Lactobacillus strains produce enzymes involved in mannose metabolism which potentially contribute to detoxification.
source: Bombilactobacillus and Lactobacillus strains also produce enzymes involved in mannose metabolism which potentially contribute to this detoxification mechanism (Zheng et al., 2019; Ellegaard et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Genomes of Bifidobacterium strains harbor a wider repertoire of glycoside hydrolases than other core members of the bee gut microbiota, but lack pectin lyase-related genes.
source: Interestingly, genomes of Bifidobacterium strains seem to harbor a wider repertoire of GHs than other core members of the bee gut microbiota, but lack PL-related genes (Zheng et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Bacterial- or fungal-derived GH3s can degrade amygdalin.
source: Other studies have shown that bacterial- or fungal-derived GH3s can degrade amygdalin.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The Gram-positive bacterium Cellulomonas fimi encodes a GH3 with activity against β-1,6-linked glycosides.
source: For example, the Gram-positive bacterium Cellulomonas fimi encodes a GH3 with activity against β-1,6-linked glycosides (Gao and Wakarchuk, 2014), similar to the linkage found in the structure of amygdalin (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Degradation of amygdalin by GH3s isolated from Rhizomucor miehei and Talaromyce leycettanus has been observed.
source: Degradation of amygdalin by GH3s isolated from Rhizomucor miehei (Guo et al., 2015) and Talaromyce leycettanus (Li et al., 2018), or by related extracellular enzymes from Aspergillus niger, has also been observed (Chang and Zhang, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Different species of mammalian gut-associated Bifidobacterium strains can grow in the presence of amygdalin, potentially due to the production of GH1 or GH3 enzymes.
source: Moreover, different species of mammalian gut-associated Bifidobacterium strains can grow in the presence of amygdalin, potentially due to the production of GH1 or GH3 enzymes (Modrackova et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Heterologous expression of wkB204-GH3 or wkB344-GH3 using E. coli led to amygdalin degradation, but to a lesser extent than what was observed for the original host.
source: In our case, heterologous expression of wkB204-GH3 (WP_254476944) or wkB344-GH3 (WP_121913979) using E. coli also led to amygdalin degradation, but to a lesser extent than what was observed for the original host.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data from heterologous expression experiments (Figure 7).

claim: There may be other carbohydrate digestive enzymes encoded by Bifidobacterium that contribute to amygdalin or prunasin metabolism.
source: Potentially, there are other carbohydrate digestive enzymes encoded by Bifidobacterium that contribute to amygdalin or prunasin metabolism (Figure 4C), or the Bifidobacterium host perform specific posttranslational modifications on this enzyme that are not achieved during heterologous expression in E. coli (Adav et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculated based on proteomics data showing multiple upregulated enzymes.

claim: The Bifidobacterium host may perform specific posttranslational modifications on the GH3 enzyme that are not achieved during heterologous expression in E. coli.
source: Potentially, there are other carbohydrate digestive enzymes encoded by Bifidobacterium that contribute to amygdalin or prunasin metabolism (Figure 4C), or the Bifidobacterium host perform specific posttranslational modifications on this enzyme that are not achieved during heterologous expression in E. coli (Adav et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation of lower degradation rates in E. coli.

claim: The GH3 enzyme appears to be secreted by Bifidobacterium strain wkB204.
source: Moreover, it seems this GH3 is secreted by Bifidobacterium strain wkB204, but, for cloning purposes, we expressed it in E. coli without a signal sequence for secretion, and, therefore, performed assays with cell lysates, which may not be optimal for characterizing enzyme activity.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assays showing amygdalin degradation in spent medium (Figure 3B).

claim: Nectar and pollen metabolites can be chemically transformed when passing through the gut, and this may influence their effects on the host and/or the microbiota.
source: As shown in other studies, nectar and pollen metabolites can be chemically transformed when passing through the gut, and this may influence their effects on the host and/or the microbiota (Koch et al., 2019; Vidkjær et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Amygdalin is absorbed systemically by bee cells.
source: Interestingly, we also found amygdalin in bee carcasses with the gut removed, suggesting that amygdalin is absorbed systemically by bee cells. This has been observed in other studies in which amygdalin was found in the bee hemolymph after oral ingestion (Hurst et al., 2014; Vidkjær et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data showing amygdalin in body carcasses (Figure 8B) and citations to previous studies.

claim: Studies in rats have found higher concentrations of hydrogen cyanide in the blood of microbiota-colonized rats than in microbiota-deprived rats or antibiotic-treated rats after oral ingestion of amygdalin.
source: Studies in rats, for example, have found higher concentrations of hydrogen cyanide in the blood of microbiota-colonized rats than in MD rats (Carter et al., 1980) or antibiotic-treated rats (Newton et al., 1981) after oral ingestion of amygdalin.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Intravenous administration of amygdalin does not lead to hydrogen cyanide formation.
source: However, intravenous administration of amygdalin seems not to lead to hydrogen cyanide formation (Jaswal and Palanivelu, 2018), which could be correlated to the lack of toxicity observed in honey bees after amygdalin injection into the hemolymph (Hurst et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The gut microbiota is a major factor driving amygdalin degradation and hydrogen cyanide release in the guts of animals.
source: These studies suggest that the gut microbiota is a major factor driving amygdalin degradation and hydrogen cyanide release in the guts of animals.
evidence: This is inferred from studies in rats and bees showing microbiota-dependent degradation.

claim: Colonization by the normal microbiota decreases the pH to about 5 in the bee gut.
source: It is important to note that colonization by the normal microbiota decreases the pH to about 5 in the bee gut (Zheng et al., 2017), and low pH can favor the degradation of amygdalin into prunasin, then prunasin into mandelonitrile, which can undergo spontaneous degradation at acidic pH to give benzaldehyde and hydrogen cyanide (Jaswal and Palanivelu, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Low pH can favor the degradation of amygdalin into prunasin, then prunasin into mandelonitrile, which can undergo spontaneous degradation at acidic pH to give benzaldehyde and hydrogen cyanide.
source: It is important to note that colonization by the normal microbiota decreases the pH to about 5 in the bee gut (Zheng et al., 2017), and low pH can favor the degradation of amygdalin into prunasin, then prunasin into mandelonitrile, which can undergo spontaneous degradation at acidic pH to give benzaldehyde and hydrogen cyanide (Jaswal and Palanivelu, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The presence of the microbiota itself, without the action of glycoside hydrolases, could favor the degradation of amygdalin into prunasin and potentially lead to the production of hydrogen cyanide.
source: Therefore, the presence of the microbiota itself, without the action of GHs, could favor the degradation of amygdalin into prunasin and potentially lead to the production of hydrogen cyanide.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the microbiota lowers gut pH, which can favor spontaneous degradation.

claim: Bees and their native microbiota seem to tolerate relatively high doses of amygdalin.
source: Although bees and their native microbiota seem to tolerate relatively high doses of amygdalin, parasites that commonly inhabit the bee gut may not fare as well.
evidence: This is supported by survival and microbiome data showing no adverse effects at field-relevant concentrations (Figure 9).

claim: There is increasing evidence that metabolites in nectar and pollen, even those considered toxic in some cases, can improve pollinator health at specific concentrations by controlling or reducing parasite loads.
source: There is increasing evidence that metabolites in nectar and pollen, even those considered toxic in some cases, can improve pollinator health at specific concentrations by controlling or reducing parasite loads (Stevenson et al., 2017; Tauber et al., 2020; Costa et al., 2010; Simone-Finstrom and Spivak, 2012; Stevenson, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Bees tend to forage on specific plants as a means of reducing colony pathogen loads.
source: Indeed, bees tend to forage on specific plants as a means of reducing colony pathogen loads (Simone-Finstrom and Spivak, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Amygdalin exposure does not reduce Crithidia infection loads in bumble bees.
source: In contrast, this does not seem to be the case for Crithidia infection in bumble bees, whose loads are not reduced after amygdalin exposure (Richardson et al., 2015), as the parasite is not susceptible to amygdalin (Palmer-Young et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The essential oil thymol can reduce Nosema spore loads in honey bees.
source: Other plant metabolites, such as the essential oil thymol, can reduce Nosema spore loads in honey bees (Costa et al., 2010; Stevenson, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The extent of protection from plant metabolites may depend on the exposure level and on the parasite being exposed.
source: Therefore, the extent of protection may depend on the exposure level and on the parasite being exposed.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that different parasites respond differently to amygdalin.

claim: Some insects, such as bees, ants, flies, and butterflies, can use a wide range of toxic secondary metabolites to medicate themselves in a therapeutic or prophylactic way.
source: Indeed, some insects, such as bees, ants, flies, and butterflies, can use a wide range of toxic secondary metabolites to medicate themselves in a therapeutic or prophylactic way (de Roode and Hunter, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous review.

claim: Honey bees typically collect secondary metabolites in plant resins, nectar, and pollen as prophylactic medication behavior to protect their colonies from parasites.
source: Honey bees typically collect secondary metabolites in plant resins, nectar, and pollen as prophylactic medication behavior to protect their colonies from parasites (Simone-Finstrom and Spivak, 2012; Erler and Moritz, 2016; Simone-Finstrom et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Monarch butterflies feed on milkweeds with high concentrations of toxic cardenolides as a therapeutic medication against parasites.
source: Similarly, Monarch butterflies feed on milkweeds with high concentrations of toxic cardenolides as a therapeutic medication against parasites (Gowler et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Monarchs can use cardenolides as a prophylactic medication by selecting oviposition sites with high concentrations of cardenolides or transferring cardenolides to eggs to reduce parasite growth in their hatching offspring.
source: Monarchs can also use cardenolides as a prophylactic medication by selecting oviposition sites with high concentrations of cardenolides (Lefèvre et al., 2012) or transferring cardenolides to eggs (Sternberg et al., 2015) to reduce parasite growth in their hatching offspring.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Some species of fruit flies use transgenerational medication to resist attack from parasitoid wasps.
source: Some species of fruit flies use transgenerational medication to resist attack from parasitoid wasps (Poyet et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Female fruit flies preferentially oviposit in media containing the alkaloid atropine, which reduces infection success of parasitoids, but also reduces fecundity.
source: Female flies preferentially oviposit in media containing the alkaloid atropine, which reduces infection success of parasitoids, but also reduces fecundity.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies on fruit fly behavior.

claim: Activities of plant-derived compounds within the host gut can be modulated by the host and/or the microbiota, to lead to the final metabolite activity.
source: More recently, a few studies have brought attention to activities of plant-derived compounds within the host gut, which can be modulated by the host and/or the microbiota, to lead to the final metabolite activity (Koch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The plant metabolite callunene, from heather nectar, can play a prophylactic role in preventing Crithidia infections in bumble bees, especially when parasite cells are present in the crop.
source: The recently described plant metabolite callunene, from heather nectar, can play a prophylactic role in preventing Crithidia infections in bumble bees, especially when parasite cells are present in the crop.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study (Koch et al., 2019).

claim: Callunene cannot play a therapeutic role in infected hosts, because host metabolism inactivates it before it reaches the hindgut where Crithidia usually establishes.
source: However, callunene cannot play a therapeutic role in infected hosts, because host metabolism inactivates it before it reaches the hindgut where Crithidia usually establishes (Koch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The glycosylation status of a nectar metabolite can directly affect its activity, with the aglycones exhibiting higher activity than the corresponding glycosylated metabolite.
source: The glycosylation status of a nectar metabolite can directly affect its activity, with the aglycones exhibiting higher activity than the corresponding glycosylated metabolite. This has been observed for the metabolites tiliaside, from linden trees, and unedone, from strawberries (Koch et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Tiliaside is a glycoside with in vivo, but not in vitro, activity against Crithidia bombi as it requires deglycosylation by host and/or microbiome enzymes during gut passage to exhibit antiparasitic activity.
source: Tiliaside is a glycoside with in vivo, but not in vitro, activity against Crithidia bombi as it requires deglycosylation by host and/or microbiome enzymes during gut passage to exhibit antiparasitic activity (Koch et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Unedone is not a glycoside and has both in vitro and in vivo activity against Crithidia bombi.
source: Unedone, on the other hand, is not a glycoside and has both in vitro and in vivo activity against C. bombi.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study (Koch et al., 2022).

claim: Unedone is first glycosylated and inactivated in the midgut by bee enzymes, then deglycosylated and reactivated in the hindgut by the microbiome.
source: Interestingly, unedone is first glycosylated and inactivated in the midgut by bee enzymes, then deglycosylated and reactivated in the hindgut by the microbiome (Koch et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Honey bees monocolonized with strains of Bifidobacterium, Bombilactobacillus, or Lactobacillus can metabolize flavonoid glycosides.
source: Kešnerová et al., 2017, demonstrated that honey bees monocolonized with strains of Bifidobacterium, Bombilactobacillus, or Lactobacillus can metabolize flavonoid glycosides.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The genomes of strains from Bifidobacterium, Bombilactobacillus, and Lactobacillus contain a diverse set of carbohydrate processing genes, including glycoside hydrolases that could be involved in the cleavage of sugar residues.
source: Indeed, genomic analyses have shown that the genomes of strains from these bacterial groups contain a diverse set of carbohydrate processing genes, including GHs that could be involved in the cleavage of sugar residues (Zheng et al., 2019; Ellegaard et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Strain-level variations in the microbiome could affect parasite persistence or establishment.
source: Strain-level variations in the microbiome could, consequently, affect parasite persistence or establishment.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of strain variation in amygdalin metabolism.

claim: Perturbation of the honey bee gut microbiota by pesticides and/or heavy metals could indirectly affect parasite success in the bee gut through changes in the metabolism of secondary metabolites by the microbiome.
source: Perturbation of the honey bee gut microbiota by pesticides and/or heavy metals (Motta and Moran, 2020b; Rothman et al., 2020; Motta et al., 2022b) could indirectly affect parasite success in the bee gut through changes in the metabolism of secondary metabolites by the microbiome.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings of this study and previous studies on microbiota perturbation.

claim: Interactions between gut microbiomes and pathogens are widespread and have repeatedly been shown for the bee gut microbiota.
source: Interactions between gut microbiomes and pathogens are widespread and have repeatedly been shown for the bee gut microbiota (Raymann and Moran, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous review.

claim: In honey bees, the core microbiota contributes to protection against RNA viruses.
source: In honey bees, the core microbiota contributes to protection against RNA viruses (Dosch et al., 2021), pathogenic bacterial infections (Steele et al., 2021; Lang et al., 2022), and the microsporidian parasite Nosema (Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In honey bees, the core microbiota contributes to protection against pathogenic bacterial infections.
source: In honey bees, the core microbiota contributes to protection against RNA viruses (Dosch et al., 2021), pathogenic bacterial infections (Steele et al., 2021; Lang et al., 2022), and the microsporidian parasite Nosema (Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In honey bees, the core microbiota contributes to protection against the microsporidian parasite Nosema.
source: In honey bees, the core microbiota contributes to protection against RNA viruses (Dosch et al., 2021), pathogenic bacterial infections (Steele et al., 2021; Lang et al., 2022), and the microsporidian parasite Nosema (Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Infection by Nosema can lead to microbiome dysbiosis.
source: Further, infection by Nosema, for example, can lead to microbiome dysbiosis (Paris et al., 2020; Rubanov et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Microbiota-conferred protection in bees may involve the host immune system and/or direct microbial interactions within the gut.
source: They may involve the host immune system (Horak et al., 2020; Kwong et al., 2017a) and/or direct microbial interactions within the gut (Steele et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Microbial metabolism of dietary components may be one mechanism through which microbiota members impact hosts or co-resident microbes.
source: Our study on amygdalin shows that microbial metabolism of dietary components may be one mechanism through which microbiota members impact hosts or co-resident microbes.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by experimental data.
